Look for TLS-related stanzas; note that standard kubeconfig does not expose OCSP/CRL settings directly — these are controlled by the TLS library or wrapper configuration.
how_to_obtain.file_path: ~/.kube/config or /etc/ci-pipeline/kubeconfig or the path referenced by $KUBECONFIG
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Presence or absence of tls-server-name, insecure-skip-tls-verify fields; absence of these fields does not confirm revocation checking is active.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Search pipeline agent configuration files and environment for OCSP or CRL settings. Many Go-based tools (kubectl, Argo CD app controller) do not natively expose revocation config; check for wrapper scripts, Java pipeline agents (Jenkins), or custom TLS configurations that set revocation flags.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -rEi 'ocsp|crl|revocation|stapling' /etc/ci-pipeline/ /opt/jenkins/ /opt/gitlab-runner/ /opt/tekton/ ~/.config/ 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Any matched lines will reveal whether OCSP/CRL is referenced; no output indicates revocation checking is likely absent (default 'none').

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Jenkins-based pipelines, inspect the Java TLS configuration. Revocation checking in the JVM is controlled by system properties such as 'com.sun.net.ssl.checkRevocation' and 'ocsp.enable' in the java.security policy file.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -E 'checkRevocation|ocsp\.enable|com\.sun\.security\.enableCRLDP' /etc/java-*/security/java.security /usr/lib/jvm/*/jre/lib/security/java.security 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lines like 'ocsp.enable=true' or 'com.sun.security.enableCRLDP=true' confirm revocation checking is active; missing or 'false' values indicate mode is 'none'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the platform engineering team to determine whether the TLS client library used by the pipeline (e.g., Go crypto/tls, Java JSSE, Python ssl) has been configured for revocation checking, and review any custom certificate validation wrappers or service mesh sidecar configurations (e.g., Envoy with OCSP stapling enabled) that may enforce revocation outside the pipeline agent itself.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A documented confirmation of which revocation mechanism (OCSP, CRL, both, or none) is active for the pipeline-to-API-server TLS connection.

typical_values: none (most common — Go's crypto/tls does not perform OCSP/CRL by default)
ocsp (configured in Java-based pipelines or Envoy sidecars with OCSP stapling)
crl (enterprise PKI environments with internal CRL distribution points)
ocsp_and_crl (high-security or regulated environments requiring dual validation)

option_description: Indicates whether an explicit maximum request body size limit is configured and actively enforced on the API gateway or load balancer sitting in front of the Kubernetes API server for the CI/CD pipeline traffic path. A value of 'true' means a payload ceiling is in effect; 'false' means no limit is enforced at the gateway layer.
security_impact: The Rego rule 'oversized_manifest_payload_causing_control_plane_disruption' fires when both 'api_gateway_payload_limit_enforced' is false/zero AND 'admission_webhook_manifest_size_validation' is false — a low-criticality (score 2) exposure mapped to T1059.013 and T1027.009. Without a payload size ceiling, an attacker or malfunctioning pipeline can submit extremely large JSON/YAML manifests (e.g., manifests with embedded multi-megabyte ConfigMap data or deeply nested structures) that exhaust API server memory and parsing capacity. This can degrade control-plane availability, delay legitimate deployments, and in extreme cases force the API server into error states where admission controllers are bypassed.

how_to_obtain.instruction: If Kong Gateway is used, query the Kong Admin API to list route or service plugins for the request-size-limiting plugin applied to the Kubernetes API server upstream.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s http://localhost:8001/routes | jq '.data[] | select(.name | test("kube|api-server")) | .id' | xargs -I{} curl -s http://localhost:8001/routes/{}/plugins | jq '.data[] | select(.name == "request-size-limiting") | .config'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A JSON object with 'allowed_payload_size' set to a non-zero value (e.g., 8 for 8MB); empty result or missing plugin indicates no limit is enforced.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For NGINX-based API gateways or Ingress controllers, inspect the NGINX configuration for the 'client_max_body_size' directive in the server or location block handling API server traffic.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -rn 'client_max_body_size' /etc/nginx/ /etc/ingress-controller/ 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A line such as 'client_max_body_size 8m;' confirms a limit; '0' or absence of the directive means unlimited body size.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check kube-apiserver flags for built-in inflight request limits and any max request body size flags. Inspect the running kube-apiserver process arguments directly.
how_to_obtain.command: ps aux | grep kube-apiserver | tr ' ' '\n' | grep -E 'max-request|max-mutating|max-inflight|request-timeout'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Flags like '--max-requests-inflight=400' confirm throttling; absence of body size flags means the API server itself imposes no explicit payload ceiling beyond Kubernetes defaults (~3MB for etcd objects).

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Envoy-based gateways (including Istio ingress), retrieve the route configuration from the Envoy admin API and check for per_route_config or http_filters with max_request_bytes set.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s http://localhost:15000/config_dump | jq '.. | objects | select(.max_request_bytes?) | {route: .name, max_bytes: .max_request_bytes}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: An object with 'max_bytes' set to a positive integer confirms enforcement; no matching objects indicates the limit is not configured.

typical_values: false (most common — API gateways in front of kube-apiserver often omit explicit payload limits)
true (configured in regulated environments or where Kubernetes API is exposed beyond the cluster network)

option_description: Indicates whether a validating admission webhook — such as an OPA Gatekeeper ConstraintTemplate or a Kyverno ClusterPolicy — is configured to inspect incoming manifest payloads and reject those exceeding a defined size threshold before the API server commits them to etcd processing.
security_impact: The Rego rule 'oversized_manifest_payload_causing_control_plane_disruption' requires BOTH 'api_gateway_payload_limit_enforced' and 'admission_webhook_manifest_size_validation' to be false before firing, making this attribute a compensating control. When both are absent, oversized manifests reach full API server processing and etcd write paths. Admission webhook size validation provides a defense-in-depth layer that catches oversized payloads that bypass gateway controls — particularly important for T1027.009 (Embedded Payloads), where an attacker embeds large binary or encoded data within seemingly valid manifest fields like annotations or ConfigMap data sections.

how_to_obtain.instruction: List all ValidatingWebhookConfigurations in the cluster and inspect their rules for size-related admission logic.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get validatingwebhookconfigurations -o json | jq '.items[] | {name: .metadata.name, rules: .webhooks[].rules}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Any webhook with rules matching 'CREATE'/'UPDATE' on '*' or specific resource types may include size validation; follow up by reviewing the webhook endpoint's policy logic.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query OPA Gatekeeper ConstraintTemplates for size-related Rego rules, and list active Constraints derived from them.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get constrainttemplates -o json | jq '.items[].spec.targets[].rego' | grep -i 'size\|length\|byte\|limit'; kubectl get constraints --all-namespaces 2>/dev/null | grep -i size
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Rego code referencing 'object_size', 'byte_length', or annotation size checks confirms size validation; no output suggests no size constraint is enforced.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Search Kyverno ClusterPolicies and Policies for rules that validate manifest payload size using JMESPath or pattern matching on resource sizes.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get clusterpolicies,policies --all-namespaces -o json 2>/dev/null | jq '.items[] | select(.spec.rules[]?.validate?) | {name: .metadata.name, rules: [.spec.rules[] | select(.validate?) | {ruleName: .name, pattern: .validate.pattern, deny: .validate.deny}]}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Policies with deny conditions referencing annotation count, data field count, or explicit size thresholds confirm validation is active.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use the Kubernetes API server's dry-run endpoint to submit a synthetically oversized manifest and observe whether an admission webhook rejects it with a size-related error message.
how_to_obtain.command:
kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f /dev/stdin <<'EOF'
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: size-test
  namespace: default
  annotations:
    test: "$(python3 -c 'print("A"*1048576)')"
data: {}
EOF
how_to_obtain.expected_output: An error response from a webhook with a message referencing size limits confirms 'true'; successful dry-run application indicates no size admission control is active.

typical_values: false (default — most clusters do not ship size validation policies out of the box)
true (configured in security-hardened clusters using OPA Gatekeeper or Kyverno with custom size policies)
